issues.legal_issue: A municipal corporation may remove a structure projecting beyond the regular line of a public street and obtain the strip of land added to the street through deemed vesting.
material_facts: A final development plan specified the future width or line of the road, and the landowners’ buildings or parts of buildings projected beyond that line.
The landowners had received building permission on plans requiring them to leave land for road widening and were aware of the proposed road line.
The municipal corporation issued notices to implement the road plan under the statutory power regulating building lines.
issues.conclusion: The municipal corporation may give notice to remove a projecting structure, including an existing structure, and may remove it; when the structure is removed or a notice requires it to be set back on rebuilding, the land added to the street is deemed part of the public street and vests in the corporation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 305 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 authorizes removal in the specified circumstances, including when a projecting part is external to the main building and when the greater portion of a building projects beyond the street line or a material portion of a projecting part has been taken down, burned down, or fallen down. Its plain language imposes a removal mandate on the corporation; vesting follows by statutory deeming without a separate possession provision. The Court applied Municipal Corporation, Indore v. K.N. Palsikar on automatic vesting and distinguished State of U.P. v. Hari Ram, which concerned a different statutory scheme. It also relied on the principle that courts do not supply omissions where the statutory language is clear, as discussed in Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Parson Tools & Plants and Punjab Land Development & Reclamation Corporation v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court.

rule.if: municipal_street_line_proceeding and final_plan_fixes_street_line and structure_projects_beyond_line and (structure_is_removed or setback_notice_on_rebuilding)

predicates.municipal_street_line_proceeding: A municipal corporation acts to regulate the line of a public street.
predicates.final_plan_fixes_street_line: A finalized planning instrument fixes the existing or future line of the public street.
predicates.structure_projects_beyond_line: A building or part of a building extends beyond the fixed street line.
predicates.structure_is_removed: The projecting building or part is removed.
predicates.setback_notice_on_rebuilding: The corporation gives notice requiring the building to be set back when it is rebuilt.

issues.definition: When a municipal corporation acts on a finalized street line and a structure projects beyond it, removal or a rebuilding setback notice causes the projecting structure to be removable and the added land to vest in the municipality.

issues.legal_issue: The special procedure for regulating the line of a public street displaces general statutory land-acquisition procedures for removing projections and does not require acquisition under a later general land-acquisition statute.
material_facts: The municipal corporations acted to widen public streets in accordance with finalized development plans and remove structures falling within the planned street lines.
The landowners argued that the corporations had to acquire the land under general acquisition provisions or the later land-acquisition statute.
The statutory scheme separately provided for compensation for damage or loss and a process to dispute compensation.
issues.conclusion: For action within the scope of the public-street-line provision, the corporation need not use the general acquisition procedures in sections 78 and 79 of the 1956 Act or acquire the land under the 2013 Act; the special compensation and dispute procedures apply instead.
issues.legal_principle: Section 305 is a special provision for maintaining the regular line of a public street and prevails over the general acquisition procedures in sections 78 and 79 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. Compensation is governed by sections 305 and 306, with disputes addressed under section 387, which provides for determination by a panchayat and, where applicable, the District Court applying the procedure of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court also considered section 56 of the Madhya Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act, 1973 and applied the special-over-general principle, including the authorities discussed in Venkateshwar Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra State Board of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education v. Paritosh Bhupesh Kumar Sheth.

predicates.public_street_line_proceeding: A municipal corporation acts to regulate a public street’s line.
predicates.action_removes_projection_within_fixed_l: The proposed action removes a structure projecting within a line fixed for the public street.
predicates.special_compensation_process_available: The applicable statutory scheme provides compensation and a process for adjudicating disputes about it.

issues.definition: When a municipal corporation removes a projection within a fixed public-street line and a special compensation process is available, the general land-acquisition procedure is not required.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory scheme for street-line removal and compensation is not unconstitutional merely because compensation may be determined after vesting or is not fixed by reference to the later general land-acquisition statute.
material_facts: The statutory scheme required reasonable compensation for damage or loss from setting back a building and compensation for land included in a public street.
If compensation was not agreed, the statute provided for adjudication and for the District Court to follow the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 procedure in relevant cases.

The landowners challenged the scheme as arbitrary, discriminatory, and inconsistent with constitutional protection of property, and sought compensation before removal or incorporation of the land into the street.
issues.conclusion: Sections 305, 306, and 387 are not invalid on the grounds raised; compensation need not be paid before removal and vesting, but must be determined and paid within a reasonable time, and the adequacy of compensation may be pursued through the statutory process.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 14 and 300A require deprivation of property to be authorized by law and the governing law to be just, fair, and reasonable; the compensation cannot be illusory. Sections 305, 306, and 387 provide for reasonable compensation and a mechanism for its adjudication, so the Court declined to strike them down or read the 2013 land-acquisition statute into them. The Court relied on K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, Rajiv Sarin v. State of Uttarakhand, and Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad v. State of Gujarat, and distinguished Laxmi Devi v. State of Bihar, which concerned an express pre-possession payment requirement in a different statute.

predicates.constitutional_property_deprivation_chal: A person challenges a statutory process that deprives them of property for a public purpose.
predicates.street_line_removal_under_law: A municipal corporation removes a projection under a law governing the line of a public street.
predicates.reasonable_compensation_provided: The law provides compensation for the relevant damage, loss, or land included in the street.
predicates.compensation_dispute_adjudication_availa: The law provides an adjudicative process for resolving disputes about compensation.

issues.definition: A property-deprivation challenge does not invalidate a street-line removal process that provides reasonable compensation and adjudication merely because payment is not required before removal.

issues.legal_issue: A finalized development plan fixing a public street’s line may be implemented without a further town-development scheme where no additional micro-planning is required.
material_facts: The road lines and widths had been specified in finalized development plans prepared and published after the statutory process for objections and suggestions.
The plans were binding on the local authorities and landowners, and the municipal corporations acted to implement them.
For one city, a town-development scheme existed; for the other, the landowners had not pleaded that such a scheme was absent.
issues.conclusion: The finalized development plan is binding and may be implemented under the public-street-line provision; a further town-development scheme or municipal town-planning scheme is unnecessary where the plan has fixed the relevant street line and no further micro-planning is required.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 19(5) and 25 of the Madhya Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act, 1973 make a finalized development plan binding and require land use and development to conform to it. Section 292 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 prevents a duplicate municipal planning scheme where a scheme under the planning legislation applies; the relevant expression includes a regional plan, development plan, or town-development scheme. The Court relied on Chairman, Indore Vikas Pradhikaran v. Pure Industrial Coke & Chemicals Ltd. for the primacy of a final development plan, and Rajendra Shankar Shukla v. State of Chhattisgarh for the relationship between development plans and town-development schemes.

rule.if: municipal_plan_implementation_proceeding and final_plan_fixes_street_line and plan_is_binding and no_further_micro_planning_needed

predicates.municipal_plan_implementation_proceeding: A local authority acts to implement a finalized land-use plan.
predicates.final_plan_fixes_street_line: The finalized plan specifies the relevant public-street line or width.
predicates.plan_is_binding: The finalized plan binds the local authority and persons using or developing land in the planning area.
predicates.no_further_micro_planning_needed: The finalized plan resolves the relevant planning detail without further area-specific planning.

issues.definition: When a binding finalized plan fixes the street line and no further micro-planning is needed, the local authority may implement it without an additional town-development scheme.
